summaries.example: Imagine a group of children choosing a side of the playground for a game. If everyone keeps using the same side, the game works smoothly. They may never have made a formal agreement. Lewis called a repeated pattern like this a convention when people follow it because they expect others to do so and because coordinating is useful.
summaries.summary: David Lewis was a highly influential philosopher who built detailed theories across many subjects. In his first book, Convention, he argued that conventions are regular patterns that help people coordinate. For example, people may keep using the same rule because they expect others to use it too. He later explained counterfactuals—claims about what would happen under different conditions—by comparing possible worlds. Lewis also defended modal realism, the unusual view that many concrete possible worlds exist. In metaphysics, he developed Humean supervenience, the idea that broad facts such as laws and causes depend on a basic arrangement of local facts. His work aimed to show how everyday ideas could fit into a systematic picture of reality.
key_ideas: David Lewis worked in many areas of philosophy, including language, mind, science, knowledge, ethics, and metaphysics.
He explained conventions as useful patterns that solve coordination problems, not necessarily as promises or spoken agreements.
He studied counterfactuals by comparing the actual world with the most similar possible worlds.
His modal realism says that possible worlds are real, concrete worlds, although only one is the actual world.
His Humean approach tried to explain laws, causes, minds, and other complicated facts using simpler facts about the world.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lewis shows how a philosopher can connect ordinary life with big questions. Why do people use the same words? What makes a rule work? What does “could have happened” mean? How can minds and causes fit into a scientific picture? His answers were influential even when other philosophers disagreed with them. Studying his ideas helps us see that familiar practices and words can hide difficult questions.

important_terms.definition: A pattern of behavior that helps people coordinate, especially when everyone expects others to follow it.
A way something could be, even if it is not the way things actually are.
A statement about what would happen if something were different from the way it really is.
The idea that a bigger fact depends on, and is fixed by, more basic facts.

questions_to_think_about: Can a rule become a convention even if nobody officially agrees to it?
When you say something could have happened differently, what do you mean?
Should a language rule depend on what speakers do, what listeners expect, or both?

summaries.example: Suppose students repeatedly meet at one library entrance because it is convenient and everyone expects the others to arrive there. They might prefer another entrance in an ideal situation, but once the pattern is established, each student has a reason to maintain it if the others do. On Lewis’s analysis, this can be a convention without an explicit agreement. A language can work similarly: speakers generally tell the truth in that language, while hearers generally trust what they hear, creating a coordination system.
summaries.summary: David Lewis was one of the most wide-ranging philosophers of the twentieth century. The entry highlights several connected projects. In Convention, Lewis analyzes conventions as regularities that solve recurrent coordination problems. They do not require explicit agreements; people may conform because they expect others to conform and because coordination serves their interests. His account of language develops this idea through conventions of truthfulness and trust, with later revisions giving hearers a more direct role. Lewis’s broader metaphysics uses possible worlds to analyze counterfactuals, modality, and aspects of content. His modal realism says that other possible worlds are concrete, isolated worlds, and counterpart theory explains how an individual could have had different properties without existing in several worlds. His Humean supervenience attempts to show how laws, chances, causation, dispositions, and mental or linguistic facts can depend on an underlying pattern of basic facts. Lewis’s theories are ambitious, systematic, and often controversial, but they remain important because they connect formal analysis with ordinary concepts.
key_ideas: Lewis rejected the simple thought that language must come before convention because agreements are made in language. Conventions need not be agreements; they can arise as stable solutions to coordination problems.
His analysis emphasizes recurrent situations, expectations, overlapping reasons to conform, and alternative patterns that could also coordinate behavior.
In later work on language, Lewis placed more emphasis on coordination between truthful speakers and trusting hearers.
His counterfactual theory compares worlds by similarity, while allowing that there may be several equally close worlds or no single closest world.
Modal realism gives possible-world semantics an ontological interpretation: possibilities are true at concrete worlds other than the actual one.
Humean supervenience seeks to locate laws, chances, causation, dispositions, mental facts, and meanings in a basic distribution of properties and relations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Lewis’s work matters because it asks how apparently abstract or social facts can fit into a unified account of reality. Language depends on coordination, counterfactual reasoning depends on comparisons among possibilities, and scientific laws may be understood through the best systematization of facts. These proposals also clarify where philosophical disagreements begin: whether conventions require agreement, whether possible worlds are concrete, and whether causation or laws can be reduced to more basic facts. His methods influenced philosophy of language, metaphysics, epistemology, philosophy of mind, and ethics.

important_terms.definition: For Lewis, a regularity in action or belief within a recurrent coordination problem, supported by mutual expectations and reasons to conform.
A condition under which a sentence is true; Lewis often represents it as the set of possible worlds where the sentence is true.
A conditional about what would happen if its antecedent were true, often analyzed by comparing relevant possible worlds.
The relation by which higher-level facts depend on, and are fixed by, a specified lower-level base.
Lewis’s view that possible worlds are concrete realities, with possibility understood as truth at some world.
A property treated as especially suited to objective resemblance, causal explanation, or a natural description of reality.

questions_to_think_about: Does a convention require common knowledge in the ordinary sense, or can mutual expectations and reasons be enough?
Why might adding information to a counterfactual’s antecedent change its truth value?
What advantages does Lewis gain by treating possible worlds as concrete rather than abstract?
Could a language be maintained by both speaker-truthfulness and hearer-trust?
Does explaining a higher-level fact in terms of lower-level facts remove anything important, or merely locate it?

summaries.example: A school might use a particular online platform for announcements. Nobody may have voted for it, but students and teachers keep using it because they expect everyone else to look there. Another platform might have worked too, yet switching would make communication harder. Lewis would see this as a possible convention: a repeated practice supported by shared expectations and coordination, rather than necessarily by an official promise.
summaries.summary: David Lewis was a philosopher known for developing broad, carefully connected theories. A central topic in the entry is convention. Lewis argues that conventions are regularities in behavior or belief that help solve coordination problems. People keep following a pattern because they expect others to follow it, and because conformity works better than acting alone. This means a convention can exist without a formal agreement. Lewis applies the idea to language. A community’s language is supported by patterns in which speakers generally express what they believe to be true and hearers generally accept what they hear as belonging to that language. His later account gives both sides of communication a role. The entry also places this work within Lewis’s larger philosophy. He analyzed counterfactuals through comparisons among possible worlds, defended modal realism, and used counterpart theory to discuss how individuals could have been different. His Humean supervenience project sought to show how laws, chances, causes, and mental or linguistic facts could depend on a more basic arrangement of facts. These views are distinctive and debated, but together they show Lewis’s aim of giving ordinary ideas precise philosophical explanations.
key_ideas: Lewis’s theory of convention treats conventions as solutions to coordination problems. An explicit agreement is not required.
Language is a coordination practice: later versions of Lewis’s account connect truthful speaking with trusting hearing.
Lewis analyzed counterfactuals by asking which possible worlds are most similar to the actual world, while allowing that similarity may depend on context.
His theory of modal realism says that possible worlds are concrete, separate worlds, not merely ideas or descriptions.
Counterpart theory says that an ordinary thing exists in only one world but has counterparts in other worlds that can share some of its properties.
Humean supervenience tries to explain higher-level features, such as laws and causation, from a basic pattern of local facts and relations.
summaries.why_it_matters: Conventions are everywhere: language, traffic rules, classroom routines, and systems for exchanging information. Lewis helps explain why such patterns can be stable even when nobody created them by decree. His other theories matter because they connect everyday reasoning with difficult questions about possibility, explanation, and reality. Even if one rejects his conclusions, examining his arguments teaches us how philosophical theories define familiar ideas and test them against unusual cases.

important_terms.definition: A repeated pattern that solves a coordination problem because people expect others to follow it and have reasons to follow it too.
A statement describing when a sentence is true, often by listing the possible situations where it is true.
A claim about what would happen if something had been different, such as “If the alarm had rung, we would have left.”
The idea that one set of facts is fixed by another, more basic set of facts.
The view that many concrete possible worlds exist, and that a claim is possible if it is true at one of them.
An especially fundamental or objectively important property that helps determine resemblance and explanation.

questions_to_think_about: Can people follow a convention when they disagree about what would be best in an ideal situation?
Why does Lewis reject the idea that making a counterfactual’s starting condition stronger must preserve its truth?
What might be gained, and what might be lost, by saying that possible worlds are concrete?
How could a community’s expectations help determine what language it speaks?
Is causation just a pattern of counterfactual dependence, or is it something more basic?
